subject: Physics
central_question: How do semiconductor energy bands, charge carriers, doping and p–n junctions enable diodes to control and rectify electric current?
in_scope_units: Introduction comparing vacuum-tube devices with compact, low-power and reliable solid-state semiconductor devices.
Classification of metals, semiconductors and insulators by conductivity, resistivity and energy-band structure.
Elemental and compound semiconductors, with focus on silicon and germanium.
Valence band, conduction band and energy gap in metals, insulators and semiconductors.
Intrinsic semiconductors, covalent bonding, thermal generation of electron–hole pairs, hole motion, current and recombination.
Extrinsic semiconductors, doping, donor and acceptor impurities, n-type and p-type materials, majority and minority carriers and impurity energy levels.
Formation of a p–n junction through diffusion and drift, depletion region and barrier potential.
Semiconductor diode under forward bias and reverse bias.
Diode V–I characteristics, threshold voltage, reverse saturation current, breakdown voltage and dynamic resistance.
Half-wave and full-wave rectification of alternating voltage.
Capacitor filtering of rectified voltage and the role of the RC time constant.
banned_topics: Detailed transistor operation and amplifier configurations, which are mentioned historically but are not developed in the supplied chapter text.
Digital logic gates and Boolean algebra, which are outside the supplied chapter.
Advanced semiconductor quantum mechanics beyond the simplified energy-band and carrier model used here.

known_pitfalls.claim: An n-type semiconductor is negatively charged and a p-type semiconductor is positively charged.
known_pitfalls.correction: Both materials remain electrically neutral overall; n-type and p-type identify their majority carriers.

known_pitfalls.claim: A hole is a separate positive elementary particle inserted into the crystal.
known_pitfalls.correction: A hole is an electron vacancy in a covalent bond that behaves as an effective positive carrier.

known_pitfalls.claim: A p–n junction can be made by pressing separate p-type and n-type slabs together.
known_pitfalls.correction: A proper junction requires continuous crystal contact at the atomic level and is formed within one semiconductor crystal.

known_pitfalls.claim: Reverse-biased diode current is exactly zero.
known_pitfalls.correction: A small reverse saturation current flows because of minority carriers until breakdown.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Example 14.1 to relate the energy gaps of carbon, silicon and germanium to insulating or semiconducting behaviour.
Use NCERT Example 14.2 to calculate majority and minority carrier concentrations in arsenic-doped silicon.
Use NCERT Example 14.3 to explain why physically joining separate p-type and n-type slabs does not create a proper junction.
Use NCERT Example 14.4 to calculate forward and reverse diode resistance from the V–I characteristic.
Use NCERT Exercise 14.6 to compare the output frequencies of half-wave and full-wave rectifiers.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter EXERCISES are numbered 14.1 to 14.6 and cover carrier type, dopants, band gaps, junction formation, forward bias and rectifier frequency.
